strengths: Identifies and formalizes an important security vulnerability in locate-then-edit model editing that was understudied, with significant implications for LLM safety
Strong theoretical foundation with elegant mathematical derivations (Eq. 4-5) and formal guarantees (Theorems E.13, E.16, E.21) with clearly stated assumptions
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 3 models, 3 editing methods, and 2 datasets with strong quantitative results (~99% subject recall, 88% semantic similarity)
Bidirectional contribution providing both attack (KSTER) and defense (subspace camouflage) mechanisms, demonstrating practical awareness
Well-motivated subject invariance insight (Figure 2) combining attention analysis and empirical validation that key vectors are largely prompt-invariant
Rigorous robustness analysis including covariance estimation perturbation (Theorem E.16) and extensive ablation studies on templates and covariance sources
Thoughtful failure analysis revealing bimodal failure modes (semantic generalization error vs. optimization constraint conflict) that provide insights into editing limitations
weaknesses: Restricted to single-edit setting with sequential editing explicitly deferred, significantly limiting applicability to real deployments where edits accumulate
Strong threat model assumptions requiring: predefined subject/prompt candidate pools, access to covariance matrix C, and simultaneous white-box access to both pre- and post-edit models
Stage II (prompt recovery) less rigorous than Stage I—entropy reduction is heuristic-based rather than principled, with significant performance gaps (CounterFact 50% vs. zsRE 8-40% top-1 recall)
Defense mechanism exhibits protection-utility tradeoff with degradation in metrics at higher protection levels, and AlphaEdit shows significantly greater instability than MEMIT under camouflage
Limited experimental scope to factual editing only; unclear if results generalize to other editing types or whether defense generalizes beyond spectral analysis-based attacks
Critical separation assumptions (E.5, E.6) necessary for theoretical guarantees not quantified empirically, creating theory-practice gap; optimal δθ values not reported
Candidate pool construction appears artificial (first 2,000 examples); practical threat depends on unrealistic scenarios with simultaneous model access and pre-constructed candidate pools

Rigorous mathematical framework with formally proved guarantees (Theorems E.13, E.16, E.21) and comprehensive perturbation analysis showing robustness to noisy covariance
Extensive empirical validation achieving 99%+ subject recall across three models and three editing methods with clear ablation studies
Compelling empirical evidence for subject invariance (Figure 2) showing key vectors remain consistent across prompt templates
Dual contribution providing both attack and defense with theoretical robustness guarantees (Theorems E.24-E.25)
Honest treatment of limitations and failure mode analysis (§4.4) discussing semantic ambiguity and optimization conflicts
weaknesses: Questionable threat model realism: white-box access to both pre-edit and post-edit parameters is extremely strong; this assumption fundamentally contradicts the claim that editing is a privacy-protection mechanism

Critical dependence on predefined candidate pools (Assumption E.1) severely limits applicability; paper provides no experiments on attack degradation with incomplete/biased candidate sets, and justification for constructing pools is hand-wavy

Prompt recovery performance is substantially weaker than subject recovery (50% top-1 recall on CounterFact, <40% on zsRE); Figure 4 shows bimodal failures with systematic 700-1k rank outliers indicating fundamental brittleness
Single-edit limitation fundamentally excludes real deployments; sequential editing is explicitly deferred despite being critical for practical deployment scenarios
Defense shows concerning utility degradation with AlphaEdit efficacy crashing to 0.46 at α=7 and numerical instability issues; trade-off between protection and utility is poorly balanced
Gray-box baseline performance gap is so large (0.99 vs 0.43-0.68) that it obscures whether vulnerability is in parameters vs behavior; suggests threat model conflates different attack vectors
Informal theoretical assumptions (E.5, E.6) rely on empirical observations without systematic analysis of when/why they hold or how robustly they generalize

Missing critical experiments: incomplete candidate pool robustness, adaptive attack evaluation, sequential editing scenarios, and user studies validating whether recovered prompts enable actual privacy violations

Well-motivated defense mechanism (subspace camouflage) using semantic decoys rather than noise
Comprehensive theoretical guarantees (Theorems E.13, E.16, E.21, E.24-E.25) with clear assumptions and proofs
Honest discussion of limitations and failure modes (semantic ambiguity, confused edits)
Clear presentation with excellent visualizations and reproducible experimental setup with code availability promised
Thoughtful ethical analysis and dual-use impact statement appropriate for security/privacy work

strengths: Novel vulnerability identification: First systematic study revealing that parameter updates leak edited subjects through row space analysis—a creative and practically significant insight
Sound theoretical foundation: Elegant use of Woodbury matrix identity to derive key property, with formal recovery guarantees (Theorems G.13, G.21) and defense properties (Theorems H.3-H.4)
Strong empirical validation: Comprehensive experiments across 3 models, 3 editing methods, 2 datasets with multiple runs; robustness studies on candidate pool size and covariance estimation
Novel empirical insight: Well-validated observation that key vectors remain ~95% similar across prompt templates, providing solid motivation for subject invariance assumption
Dual contribution with principled defense: Subspace camouflage constraint formulation (Eq. 9) is mathematically grounded; Theorem H.3 proves indistinguishability from original editing
Honest limitations discussion: Clearly articulates failure modes and identifies interesting phenomena (semantic ambiguity, confused edits) that reveal deeper insights about model editing
Comprehensive presentation: Well-organized with clear algorithms, extensive theoretical proofs in appendices, ablation studies, and promised code release
weaknesses: Candidate pool assumption limits threat model: Assumes ground-truth subjects in candidate sets; while robust to 10^7 candidates, this significantly constrains practical applicability and may not reflect realistic attacker capabilities

Fundamental attack limitations reduce effectiveness: ~20-30% of prompts rank outside top-20 (Figure 3); semantic ambiguity failures (rank 6-100) reveal attack limitations tied to editing method deficiencies, not just attack design

Defense-utility tradeoff is problematic: At α=5, F1 drops to 0.25-0.50 on some benchmarks (Figure 4); decoy hallucination increases from 0.51 to 0.23 TFR at α=7 (Table 17); repeated sequential application effects remain uncharacterized
Covariance matrix dependency: Requires either access to or ability to estimate C, assuming knowledge of editing data distribution—limits scenarios where attack is applicable

Prompt recovery stage is relatively straightforward: Entropy reduction metric is intuitive; Top-1 prompt recovery (33-51%) substantially lags subject recovery (99%), reducing practical utility of this stage
End-to-end degradation: Object recovery reaches only 32-35% Top-1 and 61-81% Top-20 (Table 3), suggesting cumulative information loss through the attack pipeline
Missing empirical comparisons: No direct benchmarking against Youssef et al. (2025) despite similar goals; limited comparison with gradient-based inversion approaches
Theoretical assumptions are idealized: δθ-separability (G.5) empirically motivated but not universally guaranteed; full-rank assumptions may fail in degenerate cases

strengths: Identifies an important vulnerability in locate-then-edit model editing paradigm with practical implications for LLM security
Solid theoretical analysis using Woodbury matrix identity to show row space encodes subject fingerprint; theorems G.12-G.13 are mathematically sound
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three LLMs, three editing methods, and two datasets with high attack success rates (99% subject recall, 88% semantic similarity)
Proposes both attack and defense mechanisms with theoretical robustness guarantees (Theorems H.3-H.4)
Extensive appendices with detailed proofs and derivations demonstrate rigor
weaknesses: Severely unrealistic threat model: requires attacker to have both pre- and post-edit parameters AND candidate pools; the candidate pool requirement is critical but inadequately justified—how would attackers construct realistic 1000-prompt pools for out-of-distribution edits?

Inadequate failure analysis: Figure 3 shows bimodal failure distribution with semantic generalization errors (6-100 rank) and optimization conflicts (700-1k rank), but no guidance on when attack succeeds/fails or how prevalent these cases are

Weak defense mechanism: protection-utility trade-off is substantial (Figure 4); at α=5, F1 scores collapse on several benchmarks; sequential editing behavior under defense left as future work despite being critical for real deployments

Theoretical assumptions (G.1-G.8) underexplored: subject invariance (Figure 2) validated on only 10 subjects/10 templates on one model; separation robustness lacks empirical validation; δθ-separability assumption not tested

Prompt recovery relies on ad-hoc entropy metric (Eq. 7) without justification; generic template choice lacks principled rationale; achieving top-20 recall doesn't solve practical utility given massive prompt space
Gray-box baseline substantially weaker but relegated to appendix, undermining practical relevance of white-box results
Candidate pool dependency fundamental but underexplored: ground-truth items must be in pools (Assumption G.1) or attack fails completely; paper provides no guidance on constructing realistic pools
Incomplete experimental scope: only 2000 examples per dataset; sequential editing incomplete; no computational cost analysis; missing scenarios (multi-edit targeting same subject, cross-layer edits)

strengths: Identifies an important and previously under-explored vulnerability in locate-then-edit model editing paradigms with rigorous theoretical analysis (Theorems G.13, G.16, G.21 and H.3, H.4)
Provides both attack (KSTER) and defense (subspace camouflage) with comprehensive theoretical grounding using elegant mathematical framework (Woodbury matrix identity, spectral analysis)

Comprehensive experimental validation across three LLMs (GPT-J, Llama3-8B, Qwen2.5) and two datasets with extensive ablations demonstrating robustness to candidate pool size, covariance estimation quality, and sequential editing

Strong empirical results with high success rates (~99% subject recall, 88% semantic similarity on CounterFact) and thoughtful analysis of failure modes (bimodal distribution revealing semantic ambiguity and optimization conflicts)
Clear presentation with effective organization, good use of appendices, and honest discussion of limitations and ethical implications in impact statement
Defense mechanism that maintains model utility while providing protection (Table 4: subject rank increases from 50 to 394 with minimal performance degradation at α=5)
weaknesses: Attack requires strong assumptions: candidate pools of subjects and prompts (though robustness shown), white-box access to parameter differences, and access to or ability to estimate covariance matrix C

Significant theory-practice gaps: Assumption G.5/G.6 on δθ-separability violated in practice (Figure 2b shows cosine similarities >0.95 between edited and non-edited subjects); bimodal failure distribution (Figure 3) represents fundamental limitations
Prompt recovery has inherent limitations with only ~50% Top-1 recall on CounterFact, and significant degradation on QA-style datasets (Top-1 recall 0.08-0.40 on zsRE in Table 2)

Defense introduces new failure modes: hallucinations increase substantially with protection level (Table 17: True Fact Recall drops from 0.51 to 0.23 at α=7) and scalability under sequential editing remains unvalidated

Limited experimental scope: relatively small batch sizes (N≤100), no comparison to alternative defense mechanisms (differential privacy, randomization), and gray-box baseline using Jensen-Shannon divergence is weak

Missing analysis on design choices: entropy reduction formulation (Eq. 7) not well justified, decoy subject quality effects unexplored, and practical guidance for selecting α given utility-protection trade-offs unavailable
